estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases

estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases
estimates.notes: One study in the review (Hu et al.) provided approximate median infectious period of 6.5–9.5 days for asymptomatic infections based on time to two consecutive negative RT-PCR tests.

estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases
estimates.notes: Mean 13.4 days (95% CI 10.9–15.8) from symptom onset to first of two negative RT-PCR tests, pooled across 15 virological studies (high heterogeneity I²>75%). RT-PCR positivity outlasts true infectious potential by approximately 2–6 days; viral culture studies indicate most transmission ceases by day 8–10 post-symptom onset.

estimates.population: Mild-to-moderate symptomatic cases — viral culture / true infectiousness
estimates.title: The duration of infectiousness of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2
estimates.notes: Rapid review integrating viral culture, contact tracing, and viral shedding data. Concluded that mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients are highly unlikely to remain infectious beyond 10 days post-symptom onset; most transmission occurs earlier. Viral culture success (the gold-standard infectiousness proxy) drops sharply after day 8. Note: this is a lower estimate than the Byrne et al. RT-PCR-based figure above because culture positivity declines faster than PCR positivity.

estimates.title: Case fatality rate of COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis

estimates.title: Infection fatality rate of COVID-19 inferred from seroprevalence data
estimates.notes: Systematic review/evidence synthesis of seroprevalence studies and national estimates available through 9 September 2020. Included 61 studies (74 estimates) plus 8 preliminary national estimates. Across 51 locations, the median inferred COVID-19 infection fatality rate (IFR) was 0.27%, with a corrected median of 0.23%. Reported IFRs ranged from 0.00% to 1.63% (corrected range 0.00% to 1.54%). Reflects largely ancestral / early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2 before later variants became dominant.

estimates.population: All ages, China, age-stratified (0% in <10y to 14.8% in 80+y)
estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: Overall CFR 2.3% (1023 deaths / 44,672 confirmed cases). No deaths in age <10y. CFR 14.8% in 80+y. CFR 0.9% in those with no comorbidities vs 49% case fatality in critical cases. Age-stratified CFRs: 10–19y 0.18%, 20–49y 0.32%, 50–59y 1.3%, 60–69y 3.6%, 70–79y 8.0%, 80+y 14.8%.

estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: Verity et al. estimated IFR 0.66% (95% CI 0.39–1.33%) using age-stratified CFR from China plus 1,334 individual cases identified outside mainland China. Imperial College London adjusted this to 0.9% (95% CrI 0.4–1.4%) for the UK, accounting for non-uniform attack rate.

estimates.population: All ages, Iceland — highest per-capita testing rate globally at time of report
estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: 10 deaths in 1,798 confirmed cases (CFR 0.56%). Assuming 1% of population (364,000) infected gives IFR ~0.3%. Authors note Iceland's test-and-quarantine measures may have shielded elderly, and lag between infection and death means estimates may shift. Considered the most reliable early IFR estimate due to Iceland's near-complete population testing.

estimates.title: Estimating the infection fatality rate of emerging diseases using a regression approach applied to global COVID-19 cases
estimates.notes: Regression-based estimate of the global infection fatality rate (IFR) for early COVID-19 using case fatality rates and population testing data across 139 countries affected before May 2020. Estimated a conservative global IFR of 0.90% (95% CI 0.70–1.16%). Reflects largely ancestral / early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2.

estimates.notes: Systematic review of 12 studies reporting social contact patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic. During the initial mitigation period in spring 2020, most study settings reported mean contact rates between 2 and 5 contacts per person per day, compared with pre-COVID rates of 7 to 26 contacts per person per day. Reflects contact behavior under lockdown / suppression measures rather than intrinsic baseline contact rates.

estimates.title: Nationally Representative Social Contact Patterns among U.S. adults, August 2020-April 2021
estimates.notes: National probability survey of U.S. adults with self-reported daily contacts. Mean daily contacts were 13.9 (baseline, Aug–Dec 2020) and 14.5 (follow-up, Mar–Apr 2021). This reflects contact behavior after the earliest lockdown period and under evolving mitigation measures, not pre-pandemic baseline contact rates.

estimates.notes: Contact survey conducted in March 2020 after lockdowns were lifted in Chinese provinces outside Hubei. Participants reported 2.3 contacts per day (IQR 1.0–3.0), suggesting that contact behavior remained strongly reduced even after formal lockdown ended.

estimates.title: Quantifying the risk of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection over time
estimates.notes: Systematic review of 11 large cohort studies of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection. Reinfection remained uncommon, and no clear evidence of waning was observed over follow-up periods extending to more than 10 months in several studies. Useful as an estimate of at least ~10 months of protection against reinfection during the early pandemic.

estimates.title: The prevalence of adaptive immunity to COVID-19 and reinfection after recovery – a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 54 studies from 18 countries. Around 90% of recovered individuals retained evidence of immunological memory at 6–8 months after recovery, and reinfection prevalence remained low. Good source for a conservative lower-bound estimate of post-infection immune duration.

estimates.title: SARS-CoV-2 reinfections: Overview of efficacy and duration of natural and hybrid immunity
estimates.notes: Narrative review summarizing evidence that natural immunity after SARS-CoV-2 infection provides strong protection against reinfection for at least one year, with only moderate waning before Omicron. Protection against severe disease appears to last longer than protection against infection.

estimates.title: Durability of Vaccine-Induced and Natural Immunity Against COVID-19: A Narrative Review
estimates.notes: Narrative review summarizing studies of waning protection after infection and vaccination. Reports high protection from prior infection over at least 7 months in meta-analyses and several studies showing little significant waning through roughly 8–12 months in pre-Omicron settings.

estimates.title: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection: A systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 350 studies. Estimated that 35.1% of SARS-CoV-2 infections never developed clinical symptoms and were therefore truly asymptomatic. Distinguished asymptomatic infections from presymptomatic infections and removed index cases to reduce bias.

estimates.title: Occurrence and transmission potential of asymptomatic and presymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections: A living systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Living systematic review and meta-analysis of 79 studies. Estimated that 20% of SARS-CoV-2 infections remained asymptomatic throughout infection. Prediction interval was wide because of substantial heterogeneity and risk of selection bias across studies.

estimates.title: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection by Age: A Global Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Global systematic review and meta-analysis of studies conducted during 2020 before routine vaccination. Across 14,850 infected individuals, 44.1% remained asymptomatic throughout infection. Also found strong age variation, with asymptomatic infection more common in children and younger adults than in the elderly.

WRONG DENOMINATOR FOR THIS FIELD: this is cumulative silent infection across a decade of repeated exposure, not the silent share of a given infection, and the authors note these events may be minimal or atypical rather than truly asymptomatic.

estimates.population: Unvaccinated patients aged 11 and over with no known chickenpox history, hospital serology
estimates.title: Assumptions and Realities: Unraveling Varicella Zoster Virus Immunity in Unvaccinated Populations
estimates.notes: 83.6% of 613 unvaccinated patients with no known varicella history were VZV IgG positive, rising with age. DO NOT USE AS AN ASYMPTOMATIC FRACTION — this is lifetime seroprevalence among adults whose childhood illness is decades past, so it is dominated by recall decay, and the cohort was selected for comorbidity or immunosuppression.

estimates.title: Epidemiology of Pertussis After the COVID-19 Pandemic: Analysis of the Factors Involved in the Resurgence of the Disease in High-, Middle-, and Low-Income Countries
estimates.notes: Review article summarizing published epidemiologic evidence. Reports that pertussis has an estimated basic reproduction number (R₀) of approximately 12–17, highlighting its high transmissibility. Does not derive a new R₀ estimate.

estimates.country: Finland, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, United Kingdom
estimates.title: Incidence and Reproduction Numbers of Pertussis: Estimates from Serological and Social Contact Data in Five European Countries
estimates.notes: Estimated R₀ using serological data combined with POLYMOD social contact matrices. Country-specific estimates ranged from 5.3 to 5.9, with an overall value around 5.5.

estimates.title: Expert consultation on pertussis
estimates.notes: ECDC expert consultation summarizing consensus that pertussis is highly contagious with a basic reproduction number (R₀) of 15–17. This value reflects historical transmission in a fully susceptible population and is intended for public health guidance rather than representing a new modeling estimate.

estimates.title: Bordetella pertussis: Infectious substances pathogen safety data sheet
estimates.notes: The estimated basic reproductive number (Ro) of B. pertussis, which is the expected number of secondary cases arising from a primary case in a completely susceptible population, is 12-17

estimates.title: Estimation of the Underlying Burden of Pertussis in Adolescents and Adults in Southern Ontario, Canada
estimates.notes: Age-structured transmission model calibrated to pre-vaccine (1880–1929) and vaccine-era (1993–2004) pertussis data from Southern Ontario. Estimated a basic reproduction number (R₀) of approximately 10.6 with seasonal variation from 9.9 to 11.5. The study concluded that infections in individuals with waning immunity drive most transmission to children.

estimates.title: Pertussis
estimates.notes: Infectious for about 3 weeks, from the catarrhal stage (about 1 week) through the paroxysmal cough stage (about 2 weeks) in an untreated patient. If antibiotics are initiated, the period of infectiousness is usually ≤5 days after onset of treatment.

estimates.title: Factsheet about pertussis

estimates.title: Whooping cough

estimates.title: Whooping Cough (Pertussis)

estimates.title: The social life of infants in the context of infectious disease transmission; social contacts and mixing patterns of the very young
estimates.notes: The average number of daily contacts for an infant was 6.68 overall and 5.7 for those aged ≤10 weeks.

estimates.notes: Review of published evidence concluded that infection-acquired immunity against pertussis wanes after approximately 4–20 years.

estimates.title: Clinical Overview of Pertussis
estimates.notes: CDC states observational studies suggest immunity lasts 4–20 years but is not lifelong.

estimates.population: Laboratory-confirmed household contacts of pertussis cases
estimates.title: Asymptomatic Infection and Transmission of Pertussis in Households: A Systematic Review
estimates.notes: Twenty-four studies reported laboratory-confirmed asymptomatic infections among household contacts. Asymptomatic infections comprised up to 55.6% of laboratory-confirmed contacts. The review did not report a pooled asymptomatic proportion.

estimates.population: Acellular pertussis-vaccinated adolescents during a high school outbreak
estimates.title: Longitudinal Assessment of Asymptomatic Infection of Bordetella pertussis Among Pertussis Acellular Vaccinated Adolescents
estimates.notes: Nine of 15 laboratory-confirmed infections remained asymptomatic (60%). The reported 1.7% represents prevalence in the entire study population, not the asymptomatic fraction among infected individuals.

estimates.title: Estimates of the reproduction number for seasonal, pandemic, and zoonotic influenza: a systematic review of the literature
estimates.notes: Systematic review of 111 studies. For seasonal influenza, 24 studies reported 47 reproduction number (R) estimates. Median R = 1.28 with an interquartile range (IQR) of 1.19–1.37.

estimates.population: General population during the 2009 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 epidemic
estimates.title: Estimation of the reproduction number of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 in South Korea using heterogeneous models

estimates.title: Estimation of the reproduction number of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 in South Korea using heterogeneous models

estimates.title: Influenza

estimates.title: Incubation periods of acute respiratory viral infections: a systematic review

estimates.title: Incubation periods of acute respiratory viral infections: a systematic review
estimates.notes: Same review as above; median incubation period of 0.6 days (95% CI 0.5-0.6) reported for influenza B, notably shorter than influenza A.

estimates.title: Influenza
estimates.notes: Cites the same Lessler et al. systematic review (median incubation 1.4 days for influenza A, 0.6 days for influenza B), confirming this figure remains the standard reference as of 2022.

estimates.title: How Flu Spreads
estimates.notes: CDC states symptoms typically begin about two days (range 1-4 days) after influenza virus infects a person's respiratory tract. Also notes people can be contagious starting ~1 day before symptom onset, and remain contagious through 5-7 days after becoming sick, with the first 3 days being most contagious.

estimates.title: How Flu Spreads
estimates.notes: CDC states influenza viruses can be detected beginning one day before symptoms develop and up to five to seven days after becoming sick, with people most contagious during the first three days of illness.

estimates.title: Contagious Period for Influenza (Flu)
estimates.notes: States the contagious period generally lasts from about a day before symptoms appear to up to 7 days after becoming ill; longer in people with weakened immune systems.

estimates.title: 2023-2024 Influenza Season Summary: Severity Assessment, Burden and Burden Prevented
estimates.notes: CDC estimated 40 million symptomatic illnesses and 28,000 deaths for the 2023-2024 season (~0.07% symptomatic CFR). Adults 65+ accounted for only 8% of medical visits but 68% of deaths.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: Wong, Kelly, Ip, Wu, Leung & Cowling, Epidemiology. Systematic review of 77 estimates from 50 studies on the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. When the denominator was total infections (including asymptomatic/subclinical), point estimates ranged from 1-10 deaths per 100,000 infections (0.001%-0.01%) — comparable in magnitude to seasonal influenza IFR estimates.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: When the denominator was symptomatic cases, point estimates ranged from 0-1,200 deaths per 100,000 symptomatic cases (0%-1.2%). Risk based on symptomatic cases increased substantially with age. This is roughly an order of magnitude higher than infection-based estimates and reflects the exclusion of asymptomatic/mild infections from the denominator.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: When the denominator was laboratory-confirmed cases only, point estimates ranged from 0-13,500 deaths per 100,000 confirmed cases (0%-13.5%) — the highest and most heterogeneous set of estimates, since testing was typically reserved for more severe presentations, inflating apparent severity. Authors caution this reflects a strong ascertainment bias rather than true disease severity.

estimates.population: Children and adults, longitudinal serology cohorts
estimates.title: Age-specific differences in the dynamics of protective immunity to influenza
estimates.notes: Ranjeva et al., Nature Communications. Fitted mechanistic models to longitudinal serology found protection against circulating strains wanes to half of peak levels 3.5-7 years after infection, waning faster against H3N2 than H1N1pdm09.

estimates.title: Impact of viral drift on vaccination dynamics and patterns of seasonal influenza
estimates.notes: Transmission-dynamic model exploring duration of natural-infection-induced immunity across 4, 6, and 8-year assumptions to reproduce observed seasonal epidemic patterns.

estimates.title: Review Article: The Fraction of Influenza Virus Infections That Are Asymptomatic: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Point estimates from outbreak investigations with virologic confirmation fell mostly in the 4-28% range, pooled mean 16% (95% CI 13-19%), low heterogeneity.

estimates.title: Review Article: The Fraction of Influenza Virus Infections That Are Asymptomatic: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Studies conducted across epidemics using serologic evidence of infection, adjusted for background rates of illness from other causes, reported more consistent estimates in the 65-85% range.

estimates.title: The Spectrum of Influenza in Children
estimates.notes: 6.6% of PCR/serologically-confirmed influenza infections in children were asymptomatic, increasing with age (1.7% in infants to 9.1% in ages 5-14). Asymptomatic infection is much less common in children than the ~50%+ often reported in adults.

estimates.population: Invasive disease, C:P1.5-1,10-8:F3-6:ST-11(cc11) strain, entire dataset
estimates.title: Estimates of the reproductive numbers and demographic reconstruction of outbreak associated with C:P1.5-1,10-8:F3-6:ST-11(cc11) Neisseria meningitidis strains
estimates.notes: Lo Presti et al., Infection, Genetics and Evolution. Bayesian method applied to whole-genome-sequenced isolates from invasive MenC disease, 2012-2017, including the Tuscany outbreak. R0 = 1.31 (95% HPD: 1.03-1.64) for the full dataset.

estimates.title: Estimates of the reproductive numbers and demographic reconstruction of outbreak associated with C:P1.5-1,10-8:F3-6:ST-11(cc11) Neisseria meningitidis strains
estimates.notes: R0 = 1.22 (95% HPD: 0.90-1.64) estimated from the first of two genomic subsets analyzed.

estimates.title: Estimates of the reproductive numbers and demographic reconstruction of outbreak associated with C:P1.5-1,10-8:F3-6:ST-11(cc11) Neisseria meningitidis strains
estimates.notes: R0 = 1.4 (95% HPD: 0.91-1.9) estimated from the second genomic subset, corresponding to the Tuscany outbreak period. An effective reproduction number R(t) was also estimated separately, rising to an average of 3.22 in 2015 before declining below 1 from 2016 onward following a vaccination campaign — that time-varying R(t) data would fit better as a distinct outbreak-specific parameter if your schema tracks Rt separately from R0.

estimates.population: General population, serogroup C meningococcal disease
estimates.title: Dynamic Models of Meningococcal Carriage, Disease, and the Impact of Serogroup C Conjugate Vaccination
estimates.notes: Trotter, Gay & Edmunds, American Journal of Epidemiology. Age-structured, dynamic compartmental model of carriage and disease, fitted to epidemiologic surveillance data from England and Wales prior to serogroup C conjugate vaccine introduction. Basic reproduction number estimated at 1.36, closely matching the genomic/phylodynamic estimates (1.22-1.4) from the 2020 Lo Presti et al. Italian outbreak study — good convergence across very different estimation methods.

estimates.title: Meningococcal Disease (Bacterial Meningitis) Fact Sheet
estimates.notes: Pennsylvania Department of Health states the incubation period is three to four days, with a range of two to ten days.

estimates.title: Meningococcal Invasive Disease
estimates.notes: Arizona Department of Health Services lists incubation period as 1-10 days.

estimates.title: Emergency Preparedness and Response
estimates.notes: CDC Health Alert Network states incubation period from exposure to symptoms is usually 2 to 10 days, with symptoms then progressing over several hours to several days. Used a slightly wider window than the more commonly cited 1-10 day range.

estimates.population: Cases of invasive meningococcal disease, treated
estimates.title: Meningococcal Disease Quicksheet
estimates.notes: Cases are considered infectious from 7 days before symptom onset until 24 hours after appropriate antibiotic therapy begins, with peak infectiousness shortly before onset; value is the maximum window under prompt treatment (7 presymptomatic days plus ~1 treated day) and the range reflects how much earlier treatment truncates it. TREATMENT-TRUNCATED AND CONTROL-ORIENTED, so this is a contact-tracing lookback window rather than a natural duration of infectiousness, and it should not be pooled with untreated or carriage-based durations.

estimates.title: Meningococcal Disease (Communicable Disease Control Manual)
estimates.notes: Alaska DHSS states the infectious period lasts until meningococci are no longer present in nasal/oral discharges, usually within 24 hours after appropriate antimicrobial treatment begins.

estimates.population: General, treated invasive disease, United States
estimates.title: CDC Yellow Book: Meningococcal Disease
estimates.notes: CDC Yellow Book (2026 edition, ch. 4.12) states meningococcal disease has a case-fatality rate of 10-15% even with antimicrobial treatment, with much higher fatality if treatment is delayed. Up to 20% of survivors have long-term sequelae (deafness, amputation).

estimates.title: The Burden of Infant Meningococcal Disease in the United States
estimates.notes: Judelsohn & Marshall, Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society. Overall U.S. case fatality rate from invasive meningococcal disease is approximately 12%, despite N. meningitidis being highly antibiotic-susceptible, reflecting the disease's extremely rapid clinical course.

estimates.title: The Burden of Infant Meningococcal Disease in the United States
estimates.notes: Case fatality rate was 6% in infants aged <1 year, the lowest age-stratified rate reported, despite infants having the highest overall incidence of disease. Estimated 13 annual deaths in this age group.

estimates.title: The Burden of Infant Meningococcal Disease in the United States
estimates.notes: Case fatality rate was 9.7% in adolescents aged 14-17 years.

estimates.population: Young adults aged 18-24 years, United States, 1998-2007
estimates.title: The Burden of Infant Meningococcal Disease in the United States
estimates.notes: Case fatality rate was 13.6% in those aged 18-24 years — the highest of the three age strata reported, consistent with the general pattern of case fatality rates increasing with age. Estimated 41 annual deaths across the combined 14-24 age range.

estimates.population: Adults, vaccine-induced bactericidal antibody (proxy for immune persistence)
estimates.title: Duration of Antibody Response after Meningococcal Polysaccharide Vaccination in US Air Force Personnel
estimates.notes: Zangwill et al., Journal of Infectious Diseases. Anti-capsular antibody and bactericidal activity peaked 1 month post-vaccination and declined substantially by 2 years, but remained detectable above pre-vaccination baseline for up to 10 years.

estimates.title: Meningococcal Vaccine Recommendations
estimates.notes: CDC recommends the initial MenACWY dose at age 11-12, with a booster at age 16 specifically because protection wanes over that ~4-year interval and adolescents face highest risk in the years the booster is designed to cover. For those at sustained increased risk, CDC recommends boosters every 5 years (age 7+) or every 3 years then every 5 years (under age 7), implying an assumed protective duration in that range before meaningful waning.

estimates.population: Adolescents and adults, MenB vaccine-induced protection
estimates.title: Meningococcal Vaccine Recommendations
estimates.notes: For individuals at increased risk, CDC recommends a MenB booster 1 year after primary series completion, then every 2-3 years thereafter — suggesting CDC considers MenB-induced protection shorter-lived than MenACWY protection. During outbreaks, boosters are recommended after just 1 year (or even 6 months in some outbreak situations), reflecting more conservative assumptions about protection duration when stakes are highest.

estimates.title: Meningococcal carriage by age: a systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Christensen, May, Bowen, Hickman & Trotter, Lancet Infectious Diseases. Landmark meta-analysis of 66 European studies (1970-2007). Carriage prevalence rises from early childhood, peaks at approximately 24% around age 19, and declines in older adults.

estimates.title: Carriage as a prerequisite for invasive meningococcal disease
estimates.notes: States meningococcus is carried asymptomatically in the nasopharynx of approximately 10% of the population at any given time, with rates varying by age and social/behavioural factors.

estimates.title: The Burden of Infant Meningococcal Disease in the United States
estimates.notes: Citing a meta-analysis of 89 studies across 28 countries, peak meningococcal carriage prevalence is 23.7% at age 19 — closely corroborating the Christensen et al. (2010) Lancet ID estimate of ~24% peak carriage already in this dataset, despite drawing on a different (larger, more geographically diverse) set of underlying studies.

estimates.title: Estimating human-to-human transmissibility of hepatitis A virus in an outbreak at an elementary school in China, 2011
estimates.notes: Zhang & Lo Iacono, PLoS ONE. Used transmission tree, renewal equation, and general growth methods on a 2011 outbreak involving direct child-to-child transmission at a 698-pupil elementary school. Mean serial interval was 23.9 days (SD 20.9). Estimates were higher than typical U.S. estimates but consistent with estimates from England.

estimates.population: Men who have sex with men (MSM)
estimates.title: Estimating the critical immunity threshold for preventing hepatitis A outbreaks in men who have sex with men
estimates.notes: Modeled the 1991/1992 Sydney HAV outbreak concentrated in MSM, where sexual contact was the predominant transmission route. Found sustained epidemics cannot occur once population immunity exceeds ~70%, implying a herd-immunity threshold consistent with this R0 range.

estimates.population: People who inject drugs (PWID), North Carolina
estimates.title: Determining Herd Immunity Thresholds for Hepatitis A Virus Transmission to Inform Vaccination Strategies Among People Who Inject Drugs in 16 US States
estimates.notes: Yang, Lo, Dankwa, Donnelly, Gupta, Montgomery, Weng & Martin, Clinical Infectious Diseases. State-level dynamic transmission model calibrated to PWID outbreak surveillance data across 16 U.S. states, 2016-2020 era outbreaks. North Carolina had the lowest state-level R0 estimate at 2.2, closely matching the elementary-school outbreak R0 already in this dataset despite a completely different transmission setting and population.

estimates.population: People who inject drugs (PWID), West Virginia
estimates.title: Determining Herd Immunity Thresholds for Hepatitis A Virus Transmission to Inform Vaccination Strategies Among People Who Inject Drugs in 16 US States
estimates.notes: West Virginia had the highest state-level R0 estimate at 5.0, corresponding to a herd immunity threshold of 80% (95% CI, 78-82%) — substantially higher transmissibility than other settings in this dataset, likely reflecting dense, high-frequency direct contact networks characteristic of PWID outbreaks.

estimates.population: People who inject drugs (PWID), pooled across 16 US states
estimates.title: Determining Herd Immunity Thresholds for Hepatitis A Virus Transmission to Inform Vaccination Strategies Among People Who Inject Drugs in 16 US States
estimates.notes: Meta-analysis across all 16 state-level models yielded a pooled herd immunity threshold of 64% (95% CI, 61-68%; 90% prediction interval, 52-76%). Value shown here is back-calculated from the pooled threshold using R0 = 1/(1-threshold) as an approximation; the paper reports thresholds directly rather than a single pooled R0. Authors conclude ~80% vaccination coverage (assuming 95% efficacy) could prevent most PWID-associated HAV outbreaks.

estimates.title: Chapter 9: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: CDC's standard reference states the incubation period of hepatitis A is approximately 28 days, with a documented range of 15-50 days.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: WHO states the incubation period of hepatitis A is usually 14-28 days — a narrower 'usual' range than the CDC's commonly cited 15-50 day range with a 28-day average. The two are not contradictory: WHO's range likely reflects the typical/modal window, while CDC's wider range captures the full observed spread including outliers.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A and E
estimates.notes: Johns Hopkins Medicine states the incubation period is two to six weeks (14-42 days), consistent with but slightly narrower than the CDC's 15-50 day range. Also states the person is contagious throughout the incubation period — a looser characterization than CDC's more precise infectious-window guidance (peak shedding 1-2 weeks pre-symptom, tapering ~1 week post-jaundice), worth treating as a general-audience simplification rather than a clinical benchmark.

estimates.title: Epidemiology and Prevention of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases (Pink Book), Chapter: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: Most infectious 1-2 weeks before onset of illness.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: States infectious period is 2-3 weeks before and 1 week after onset of jaundice, matching CDC/NC DHHS guidance. People are most infectious 1-2 weeks before symptom onset, when viral concentration in stool and blood is greatest; shedding and transmission risk diminish rapidly after symptoms appear.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: CDC states acute liver failure from hepatitis A is rare, with an overall case-fatality rate of 0.5%. Infection produces self-limited disease that does not result in chronic infection or chronic liver disease, though 10-15% of patients may experience symptom relapse within 6 months.

estimates.title: Infectious Diseases: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: The case-fatality rate for hepatitis A is generally low (about 0.3%) but increases substantially with age and in people with chronic liver disease. The cited chapter reports a case-fatality rate of 1.8% among adults older than 50 years.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: ECDC states chronic infection with hepatitis A is not known to occur and that infection gives lifelong immunity to the disease.

estimates.title: How Long Does Vaccine for Hepatitis A Last?
estimates.notes: States hepatitis A vaccine provides at least 20 years of protection following the full two-dose series, and CDC does not routinely recommend booster doses for healthy individuals who complete the series, implying protection is expected to persist well beyond this window (potentially lifelong).

estimates.title: CDC Surveillance Manual, Chapter 3: Hepatitis A
estimates.notes: States that in children younger than 6 years of age, most (70%) infections are asymptomatic; in older children and adults, infection is usually symptomatic, with jaundice occurring in more than 70% of patients.

estimates.title: Hepatitis A: Epidemiology and prevention in developing countries
estimates.notes: Approximately 50% of children with hepatitis A under the age of 6 years are asymptomatic, with most of the remaining having mild symptoms, often not recognized as hepatitis. Less than 5% of children below 4 years of age and less than 10% of children between ages 4 and 6 years develop jaundice.

estimates.title: The basic reproductive number of Ebola and the effects of public health measures: the cases of Congo and Uganda
estimates.notes: Estimate of R0 is 1.83 (SD 0.06) for Congo (1995) and 1.34 (SD 0.03) for Uganda (2000).

estimates.title: The basic reproductive number of Ebola and the effects of public health measures: the cases of Congo and Uganda
estimates.notes: Estimate of R0 is 1.83 (SD 0.06) for Congo (1995) and 1.34 (SD 0.03) for Uganda (2000).

estimates.title: Estimating the Reproduction Number of Ebola Virus (EBOV) During the 2014 Outbreak in West Africa
estimates.notes: Althaus, PLOS Currents Outbreaks. SEIR model fit to WHO case and death reports through August 2014. Confidence intervals are implausibly narrow because they reflect fit uncertainty against smoothed cumulative counts rather than true epistemic uncertainty — treat the point estimate, not the interval. Guinea's epidemic was the longest-running and lowest-intensity of the three, with repeated flare-ups from community resistance to burial teams.

estimates.title: Estimating the Reproduction Number of Ebola Virus (EBOV) During the 2014 Outbreak in West Africa
estimates.notes: Highest of the three country-level estimates in this study, and the upper anchor for the consensus range. Sierra Leone's epidemic was seeded by a single funeral of a traditional healer in Kailahun that has been linked to well over a hundred subsequent cases — a textbook superspreading event, which inflates an early-phase R0 estimate relative to the typical transmission chain.

estimates.title: Estimating the Reproduction Number of Ebola Virus (EBOV) During the 2014 Outbreak in West Africa
estimates.notes: Estimated basic reproduction number (R0) for Ebola virus disease (EBOV) during the 2014 West Africa outbreak in Liberia. The study estimated R0 at 1.59, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.57–1.60. This estimate reflects transmission dynamics during the early phase of the outbreak and is specific to the Liberian outbreak context.

estimates.title: The basic reproduction number (R0) of ebola virus disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: The search yielded 2042 studies. It included 53 studies from six African countries in the systematic review providing 97 Ebola mean R0 estimates.

estimates.title: Ebola Disease Signs and Symptoms
estimates.notes: CDC's standard reference states symptoms appear 2 to 21 days after contact with the virus, with an average of 8 to 10 days. Value shown is the midpoint of that stated average window. This is the range used to set the 21-day monitoring period for exposed contacts.

estimates.title: Ebola Virus Disease in West Africa — The First 9 Months of the Epidemic and Forward Projections
estimates.notes: WHO Ebola Response Team. Mean incubation of 11.4 days fitted to patients with a single reported exposure date, notably longer than the CDC's 8-10 day general figure. The gap is most likely recall and ascertainment bias — patients reporting a single identifiable exposure skew toward discrete events like funerals rather than continuous household exposure, and the earliest exposure in a continuous window tends to get reported, lengthening the apparent incubation.

estimates.title: Incubation period of Ebola hemorrhagic virus subtype Zaire
estimates.notes: Eichner, Dowell & Firese, Osong Public Health Research and Perspectives. Fitted a distribution to 196 cases from the 1995 Kikwit outbreak, estimating mean 12.7 days (SD 4.3). The paper is the main source for the claim that a 21-day quarantine misses a small but non-zero fraction of cases; the exact fraction is sensitive to the fitted distribution and later reanalyses (notably Haas 2014) produced a wide spread of answers.

estimates.title: Time From Infection to Disease and Infectiousness for Ebola Virus Disease, a Systematic Review
estimates.notes: Standard time periods from article.

estimates.title: Time From Infection to Disease and Infectiousness for Ebola Virus Disease, a Systematic Review
estimates.notes: Proposed time periods from article.

estimates.title: Ebola Virus Disease in West Africa — The First 9 Months of the Epidemic and Forward Projections
estimates.notes: WHO Ebola Response Team reported mean time from the onset of symptoms to hospitalization, a measure of the period of infectiousness in the community.

estimates.country: Democratic Republic of the Congo / Uganda
estimates.title: The basic reproductive number of Ebola and the effects of public health measures: the cases of Congo and Uganda
estimates.notes: Chowell et al. used a mean infectious period of 5.61 days for the 1976 Congo outbreak.

estimates.title: Time From Infection to Disease and Infectiousness for Ebola Virus Disease, a Systematic Review
estimates.notes: Infectious period refers to after onset of wet symptoms to recovery.

estimates.title: Ebola disease
estimates.notes: WHO states the average case fatality rate is around 50%, having varied from 25% to 90% in past outbreaks. This is the most widely cited headline figure and the basis for the consensus block, though it aggregates across species, decades, and wildly different standards of supportive care.

estimates.population: Cases with definitive outcome, West Africa 2014
estimates.title: Ebola Virus Disease in West Africa — The First 9 Months of the Epidemic and Forward Projections
estimates.notes: WHO Ebola Response Team. 70.8% (95% CI 68.6-72.8) restricted to patients with a recorded final outcome — substantially higher than the roughly 40% obtained by dividing total reported deaths by total reported cases across the whole epidemic, because cases with unknown outcome were common and were not evenly split. This pair is the clearest illustration in the dataset of how much CFR depends on denominator choice; prefer the definitive-outcome figure for modeling severity and the crude figure only for comparing against other crude surveillance ratios.

estimates.title: Ebola haemorrhagic fever in Zaire, 1976
estimates.notes: 280 deaths among 318 cases in the index outbreak for Zaire ebolavirus.

estimates.population: Confirmed hospitalized cases with known outcome, Jui Government Hospital, Freetown
estimates.title: Age and Ebola viral load correlate with mortality and survival time in 288 Ebola virus disease patients
estimates.notes: Li et al., International Journal of Infectious Diseases 42:34-39. Retrospective series at Jui Government Hospital, Freetown, Oct 2014-Mar 2015: 288 RT-PCR-confirmed cases, 98 deaths, 36 recoveries. The 73.13% is computed on only the 134 patients with a recorded outcome; the other 154 were transferred out and lost to follow-up, so over half the cohort is missing from the denominator and the figure is likely inflated if transfers skewed toward survivors. Range shown is the age-stratified span, NOT a confidence interval: 57.58% at age <=18, 77.42% at 18-40, 79.49% at >=40. Mortality correlated with age, log viral load (OR 3.095 above 10^6 copies/ml, p = 0.004) and diarrhoea; no sex difference. Median stay was 2 days for deaths vs 14 for survivors, so much of the cohort died too quickly for supportive care to affect outcome.

estimates.title: Ebola Virus Neutralizing Antibodies Detectable in Survivors of the Yambuku, Zaire Outbreak 40 Years after Infection
estimates.notes: Rimoin et al., Journal of Infectious Diseases. Traced survivors of the 1976 Yambuku outbreak and found IgG against Ebola glycoprotein in all 14 tested, with neutralizing activity in a subset, 40 years after infection. Strongest available evidence for durable natural immunity, though the sample is tiny and serology is a correlate rather than a demonstration of protection.

estimates.title: Ebola virus disease
estimates.notes: Penn Medicine patient-information page (A.D.A.M. content, last reviewed 31 December 2023), sourced to CDC, WHO, Goldman-Cecil Medicine 27th ed. and Mandell 10th ed. States survivors are immune 'for 10 years or more' and can no longer spread the virus, and that cross-protection against a different Ebola species is not known. CONFLICTS with the ECDC entry in this parameter, which states infection confers lifelong immunity: this is the more conservative framing and closer to what the evidence supports, since the 40-year antibody persistence in the Yambuku cohort is serological rather than a demonstration of protection. Treat 10 years as a defensible floor and 'lifelong' as an upper assumption, not as two compatible readings. LOW EVIDENTIARY WEIGHT: general-audience tertiary summary, no primary data, and the 10-year figure is asserted without a cited source; use for the direction of the caveat, not as an independent estimate. The page also states men can carry virus in semen 'for as long as 3 months', which is contradicted by the Deen et al. cohort in infectious_days showing RNA positivity beyond 500 days — treat the 3-month figure as outdated.

estimates.population: Vaccinated adults, PREVAC trial (rVSV-ZEBOV and Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo)
estimates.title: Long-term cellular immunity of vaccines for Zaire Ebola Virus Diseases
estimates.notes: Wiedemann, Lhomme, Huchon et al., Nature Communications 15:7666. Immunology ancillary study of the PREVAC randomized trial (NCT02876328), 191 adults per-protocol at the Landreah site, Guinea, with a 31-participant subset followed to 60 months. Both licensed regimens induced EBOV-specific memory T-cell responses detectable at 24, 36, 48 and 60 months post-prime with NO decline over that window, which is the basis for the 1825-day floor here. Two caveats against reading this as duration of protection. (1) DURABILITY IS ASSAY-DEPENDENT: ex-vivo responses were undetectable in every arm by month 12; the persistent signal appears only after 8-day in-vitro expansion with EBOV peptide pools, so this demonstrates memory T cells can be recalled, not that circulating effector immunity persists. Antibody GMCs had already fallen by M12 to roughly pre-boost levels (433 EU/mL Ad26-MVA, 828 rVSV, 663 rVSV-booster, vs 92 placebo). (2) NO CORRELATE OF PROTECTION EXISTS for EVD, and the authors state this plainly — antibodies are thought primary for rVSV protection, CD8+ T cells for the adenovirus/MVA platforms, but the level required for lasting protection is unknown, so T-cell persistence cannot be converted into a protection duration. Platform differences: Ad26 prime induced polyfunctional CD4+ responses further boosted by MVA; rVSV induced minimal ex-vivo T-cell responses despite strong antibody titers and a D7 pro-inflammatory signature (IL-18, IP-10, TRAIL). CD4+ T-cell responses correlated with anti-EBOV IgG, which the authors offer as a rationale for eventual boosting. LOW PRECISION: the 60-month subset is 31 people (9-12 per arm), and the rVSV-booster arm had only 7-9, too few to interpret its absent CD8+ signal. Use 1825 days as a lower bound on immune memory, not as an immunity duration, and keep the vaccine and natural-infection entries in this parameter separate — they are different quantities with different evidence.

estimates.title: Impact of asymptomatic infection and acquired immunity on the spread and control of Ebola
estimates.notes: Bellan, Pulliam, Dushoff & Meyers, Lancet 384(9953):1499-1500. CORRESPONDENCE, NOT A PRIMARY ESTIMATE: the 50% figure is an illustrative modeling assumption chosen to demonstrate a structural point, not a measurement, and the range shown is the span of the two prior serological findings the letter cites (a post-outbreak serosurvey in which 71% of seropositive individuals reported no disease, and Leroy et al.'s 46% seropositivity among asymptomatic close contacts, already entered separately in this parameter). Do not count as independent evidence and do not double-count with Leroy. The substantive contribution is the modeling consequence: comparing two Liberia models with identical R0, the one ignoring asymptomatic infection projected roughly 50% more cumulative symptomatic cases by January 2015, because asymptomatic infections are unlikely to be infectious but do contribute to herd immunity. This confirms the direction flagged in the consensus block — raising this parameter makes modeled outbreaks easier to control, the opposite of the respiratory-pathogen intuition. SUPERSEDED ON MAGNITUDE: written October 2014, before Glynn et al. 2017 found roughly 3% using a validated oral-fluid assay, so the premise that a 'substantial proportion' of infections are asymptomatic is now contested. Retain for the structural argument, not the value. PMID 25390569.

estimates.title: Transmissibility and Pathogenicity of Ebola Virus: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Household Secondary Attack Rate and Asymptomatic Infection
estimates.notes: Dean, Halloran, Yang & Longini, Clinical Infectious Diseases 62(10):1277-1286. Pooled estimate that 27.1% (95% CI 14.5-39.6) of Ebola infections are asymptomatic — the central meta-analytic value, sitting between the Leroy 46% and the Glynn 3%, and roughly an order of magnitude above the latter. The interval is wide because the underlying serosurveys are few and use heterogeneous, mostly unvalidated assays; the assay problem is the substantive reason to weight Glynn more heavily despite this being the formal meta-analysis. The same paper is the source for the household secondary attack rate figures cited in average_contacts_daily: overall SAR 12.5% (95% CI 8.6-16.3), but almost all of it driven by direct contact — SAR was 0.8% (95% CI 0-2.3) without direct contact and 47.9% (95% CI 23.3-72.6) where nursing care was provided. That gradient is the most useful quantity in this study for parameterizing contact structure, and is a stronger basis for a contact model than any daily contact rate. Also found a statistically significant decline in direct-contact household SAR between 1976 and 2014 (P = .018), likely reflecting changed care and burial behaviour rather than viral change. Authors conclude surveillance and containment should suffice for control.

estimates.title: Reviewing estimates of the basic reproduction number for dengue, Zika and chikungunya across global climate zones
estimates.notes: 65 studies included; mean R0 by climate zone was 3.44 tropical, 10.29 sub-tropical, 2.03 temperate. Value is the tropical mean and range is the span of the three zone means, NOT a confidence interval.

estimates.title: A comparative analysis of three different methods for the estimation of the basic reproduction number of dengue
estimates.notes: Sanches & Massad, Ribeirao Preto 2009-2010, fitted from the initial growth phase without assuming exponential growth. Three standard methods on the same data gave numerically different answers, so read any single dengue R0 as method-plus-data.

estimates.title: The basic reproduction number R0 and effectiveness of reactive interventions during dengue epidemics: the 2002 dengue outbreak in Easter Island, Chile
estimates.notes: DO NOT USE AS A GENERAL VALUE: no prior dengue on Easter Island meant a genuinely naive population, a condition endemic settings never meet. Retained as the upper anchor on what a naive-population epidemic can do.

estimates.title: Estimating the basic reproduction number for single-strain dengue fever epidemics
estimates.notes: Khan, Hassan & Imran fitted the 2011 epidemic five ways (OLS and GLS on a vector-host ODE model; OLS, GLS and MCMC on a direct-transmission model) and every pre-control estimate fell between 2.95 and 3.08; value shown is the vector-host OLS figure of 2.9871. ROBUST POINT, WIDE INTERVAL: the range is the 95% CI from uncertainty analysis, so the cross-method agreement reflects a well-constrained fit rather than precision, and R0 was above unity with probability >99.9%.

estimates.title: The Incubation Periods of Dengue Viruses
estimates.notes: Chan & Johansson: 204 IIP observations from 35 studies fitted with censored Bayesian time-to-event models, mean 5.9 days with 95% between 3 and 10. No serotype differences detected; this is the reference estimate for the field.

estimates.title: Natural History of Dengue Virus (DENV)-1 and DENV-4 Infections: Reanalysis of Classic Studies
estimates.notes: Nishiura & Halstead reanalysis of 1920s human challenge data: 6.0 days (SD 1.4) for DENV-4, corroborating the pooled mean from a different evidence type. Incubation correlated negatively with fever duration and severity, consistent with a dose-response mechanism.

estimates.title: Clinical Features of Dengue
estimates.notes: CDC clinical guidance for health care providers. States dengue begins abruptly after a typical incubation period of 5-7 days, followed by three phases: febrile, critical, and recovery. Value shown is the midpoint of the stated typical range; the source gives no wider observed range, and standard references generally cite 3-14 days as the full span, so treat 5-7 as the modal window rather than the bounds. The same page supports other parameters in a dengue entry: roughly 1 in 4 infections are symptomatic (asymptomatic_fraction ~0.75), about 1 in 20 symptomatic patients progress to severe dengue, mortality in severe dengue can be reduced below 0.5% with prompt intravenous fluid support, and infection confers lifelong homotypic immunity but only months-to-years of heterotypic protection across the four DENV types — which means immunity_duration for dengue cannot be a single value and interacts with antibody-dependent enhancement on reinfection.

estimates.title: Dengue viremia kinetics in asymptomatic and symptomatic infection
estimates.notes: Infectiousness estimated by mosquito transmission or viral isolation ranges 1-7 days with a mean of 4-5; value is the midpoint of that stated mean. Primary infections run longer than secondary, so endemic populations sit at the low end of the band.

estimates.title: Asymptomatic humans transmit dengue virus to mosquitoes
estimates.notes: Dengue patients were infectious up to 5 d after the onset of symptoms.

estimates.title: Global dengue epidemic worsens with record 14 million cases and 9000 deaths reported in 2024
estimates.notes: WHO surveillance data for 2024: 14.1 million reported cases and 9,508 deaths, crude CFR 0.07%; WHO's own fact sheet gives over 14.6 million and more than 12,000 for the same year, which bounds how tight any dengue surveillance figure can be. A ratio of two undercounts, so use only as a crude-surveillance comparator.

estimates.population: Dengue patients admitted to a medical ICU
estimates.title: Nine fatal cases of dengue: a case series from an intensive care unit in Sri Lanka
estimates.notes: Of 1,722 ICU admissions over 30 months, 44 were dengue and 11 (25.0%) died, mainly from acute liver failure and shock. SEVERE SELECTION BIAS: an ICU denominator is compatible with the sub-1% severe-dengue figure rather than contradicting it, and neither transfers to the other's population.

estimates.population: Reported dengue cases, Region of the Americas, 2023
estimates.title: Case fatality rate due to dengue (Impact Indicator 23), End of Biennium Report 2022-2023
estimates.notes: PAHO reported a regional CFR of 0.050% for 2023 against a 2012-2018 baseline of 0.056%, during the Region's most severe epidemic on record with over 4.4 million cases; range shown is the span of the reported trend line, NOT a confidence interval. UPWARD-BIASED DENOMINATOR: 14 countries report only laboratory-confirmed cases to PASB, so true case counts are higher and the real CFR lower, and this is a programme target indicator rather than an independent measurement.

estimates.population: Homotypic — reinfection with the same serotype
estimates.title: Interactions between serotypes of dengue highlight epidemiological impact of cross-immunity
estimates.notes: Exposure to one virus induces lifelong immunity to all other members of that virus's serotype, but the interaction between serotypes is less clear.

estimates.title: Interactions between serotypes of dengue highlight epidemiological impact of cross-immunity
estimates.notes: Reich et al. fitted mechanistic models to 12,197 serotyped infections over 38 years in Bangkok and found strong evidence for cross-protection of approximately 1-3 years; 730 is the midpoint of that band, NOT a published point estimate. INFERRED FROM POPULATION DYNAMICS, so it is confounded with anything else producing multi-year serotype cycling — directionally solid, numerically soft.

estimates.population: Dengue-infected persons, pooled across definitions and designs
estimates.title: Asymptomatic dengue infection rate: A systematic literature review
estimates.notes: De Santis, Bouscaren & Flahault, 74 studies screened, mean asymptomatic proportion 54% across the 50 reporting it — well below the canonical 75% and the only formal systematic review of this parameter. UNWEIGHTED MEAN ACROSS INCOMPATIBLE DEFINITIONS: the review's central finding is that 'asymptomatic' has been used for clinically undetectable, undiagnosed and merely mild infection, so 54% pools three different quantities and should not be read as a corrected version of Bhatt.

estimates.population: Clinically undetectable laboratory-confirmed dengue infections (strict definition)
estimates.title: Asymptomatic dengue infection rate: A systematic literature review
estimates.notes: Only 8% of infections were asymptomatic under the strict definition of clinically undetectable AND laboratory-confirmed, roughly an order of magnitude below the headline figure and the single strongest challenge to the 75% in this parameter. LOWER BOUND, NOT A REPLACEMENT: requiring laboratory confirmation in a person with no symptoms selects for active cohort surveillance designs, so this is the floor on truly silent infection rather than a corrected central estimate.

estimates.title: Dengue, CDC Yellow Book 2026: Health Information for International Travel
estimates.notes: Sanchez-Gonzalez, Adams & Paz-Bailey state 40-80% of DENV infections are asymptomatic; value shown is the midpoint of that band, NOT a published point estimate.

estimates.population: General, US census divisions, multiple seasons
estimates.title: Retrospective Parameter Estimation and Forecast of Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the United States
estimates.notes: Reis & Shaman, Bayesian filtering across US census divisions and seasons gave R0 3.0 (SD 0.6).

estimates.title: Modeling epidemics caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
estimates.notes: SIRS model

estimates.title: Modeling epidemics caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
estimates.notes: model with gradual acquisition of partial immunity

estimates.population: Closed community settings including children, by region, year and subtype
estimates.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Transmission in Closed Community Settings That Include Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
estimates.notes: Estimates computed with a gamma-fitted 3.2-day serial interval standing in for the generation time: highest 1.76 (95% CI 1.62-1.83) for RSV-B and lowest 0.92 (0.92-1.0) for RSV-A, both in Caibiran, with variability between regions and years. Sub-unity values in an endemic partially immune population are effective reproduction numbers and must not be read as R0.

estimates.population: General, pooled across the published evidence base
estimates.title: What are the parameters and modes of transmission of RSV? A rapid review
estimates.notes: Rapid review using adapted systematic methods found only FOUR studies estimating RSV R0, spanning 0.92 (95% CI 0.92-1.0) to 3.0 (range 1.5-4.0). LOW WEIGHT, GREY LITERATURE: its value is as evidence that no proper meta-analysis of RSV R0 exists and the evidence base is four studies wide, not as an independent estimate.

estimates.title: Incubation periods of acute respiratory viral infections: a systematic review
estimates.notes: Lessler et al. screened 436 articles across nine respiratory viruses and pooled 38 with usable data, fitting log-normal distributions; the RSV pooled mean is 4.4 days. The reference estimate for this field, and the authors stress using the full distribution rather than the central value — right tail for quarantine policy, centre for source attribution.

estimates.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections in Neonates: A Persisting Problem
estimates.notes: States an incubation period of 4-6 days with a range of 2-8; value shown is the midpoint of the typical window. Consistent with the pooled estimate above and with adult challenge-model protocols, which use the same 4-5 day centre and 2-8 day span.

estimates.title: Respiratory syncytial virus
estimates.notes: Singapore CDA professional guidance gives a typical incubation of 5 days ranging from 2 to 8, matching the clinical reference entry exactly and sitting close to the 4.4-day pooled estimate. TERTIARY RESTATEMENT, not independent evidence — retained because national agency guidance is what contact-tracing and exclusion policy is actually written against.

estimates.title: Respiratory syncytial virus
estimates.notes: Singapore CDA gives an infectious period of 1-2 days before symptom onset to 3-8 days after; value and range are the derived total window width (4 to 10 days, midpoint 6.5), NOT published figures. CONFIRMS PRESYMPTOMATIC TRANSMISSION and is far shorter than the 11.2-day PCR shedding estimate because agency guidance is written around practical transmissibility and exclusion policy rather than detectable virus.

estimates.title: How RSV Spreads
estimates.notes: CDC states people are usually contagious for 3 to 8 days and may become contagious a day or two before symptoms appear; value and range are the derived total window (4-10 days, midpoint 6.5), NOT published figures. LONG RIGHT TAIL OMITTED FROM THE RANGE: some infants and immunocompromised people shed for 4 weeks or longer after symptoms resolve, which is the mechanism behind the prolonged shedders carrying ~30% of cumulative shedding days in the Kenya cohort.

estimates.title: Global, regional, and national disease burden estimates of acute lower respiratory infections due to respiratory syncytial virus in children younger than 5 years in 2019: a systematic analysis
estimates.notes: Li et al. estimated 33.0 million (UR 25.4-44.6 million) RSV-associated ALRI episodes and 101,400 RSV-attributable deaths globally, giving roughly 0.31% deaths per episode, with RSV behind 1 in 50 deaths in children under 5 and 1 in 28 in those under 6 months. THE GLOBAL POINT ESTIMATE HIDES A TEN-FOLD INCOME GRADIENT: range shown is the study's in-hospital CFR span from 0.1% (UR 0.1-0.2) in high-income to 1.4% (0.6-2.8) in low-income countries, a DIFFERENT DENOMINATOR borrowed to bound the spread, since no per-episode stratification is reported. DENOMINATOR IS LRTI EPISODES, not all infections, so the central value sits well above a true infection fatality rate.

estimates.population: US infants and children under 5 with RSV
estimates.title: Mortality Among US Infants and Children Under 5 Years of Age with Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Bronchiolitis: A Systematic Literature Review
estimates.notes: Bylsma et al., 42 studies: RSV CFRs ranged from 0% to 1.7% (n = 15) and all-cause bronchiolitis from 0% to 0.17% (n = 6), with higher values among premature, ICU-admitted and publicly insured children. NO POINT ESTIMATE IS DEFENSIBLE — the review found case definitions varying across ICD codes and laboratory confirmation, no study using systematic RSV testing, only 10 nationally representative studies with data ending in 2013, and just 2 covering otherwise healthy late-preterm to full-term infants.

estimates.population: Adults rechallenged with homologous strain group
estimates.title: Immunity to and frequency of reinfection with respiratory syncytial virus
estimates.notes: Hall et al. challenged 15 adults with prior natural infection using the same strain group at 2, 4, 8, 14, 20 and 26 months: about half were reinfected by 2 months and two-thirds by 8 months, every challenge infected at least a quarter of subjects, and within 26 months 73% had two or more infections. The strongest direct evidence in this parameter, but n=15, so treat the timeline as well-demonstrated and the proportions as imprecise.

estimates.title: Kinetics of the Neutralizing Antibody Response to Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections in a Birth Cohort
estimates.notes: Neutralizing antibody declined to pre-infection levels within roughly 3 months of primary infection, which the authors offer as a mechanism for rapid repeat infection. IMMUNOLOGICAL MARKER, NOT PROTECTION: no correlate of protection exists for RSV, so this is a floor on detectable humoral response rather than a duration of immunity.

estimates.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Reinfections in Children in Western Australia
estimates.notes: Median interval between RSV detections was 460 days (IQR 324-812), with reinfection most common in children whose first detection was before 6 months of age. ASCERTAINMENT-LIMITED: only reinfections severe enough to reach care are counted, so this measures the gap between detected episodes and is an overestimate of the interval between infections.

estimates.population: All ages, rural and urban household cohort
estimates.title: Incidence and transmission of respiratory syncytial virus in urban and rural South Africa, 2017-2018
estimates.notes: PHIRST cohort sampled regardless of symptoms: 32% of individuals had at least one infection, 33% of 396 infections were symptomatic, and only 2% sought care, giving an asymptomatic fraction near 0.67. Symptom-independent sampling is why this runs well above clinic-based estimates, and 10% of infected individuals had a repeat infection within the same season.

estimates.population: Healthy term infants, weekly surveillance birth cohort
estimates.title: Epidemiology of RSV infections in a birth cohort of healthy children, PREVAIL Cohort 2017-2020
estimates.notes: Of 91 PCR-identified infections under weekly surveillance, 24 (26%) were asymptomatic, 24% symptomatic but not medically attended and 50% medically attended. LOWEST ANCHOR AND AGE-SPECIFIC: infants are the most symptomatic age group, so this should not be generalized past the first two years of life.
